questions.question: How does the lecture describe `Hashtable` compared with `HashMap`?
options: Hashtable is the modern replacement for HashMap and should be preferred in new code
Hashtable is a legacy class similar to HashMap; it is thread-safe, but that synchronization adds overhead and makes it slower
Hashtable stores keys in sorted order, while HashMap does not
Hashtable compares keys with `==`, while HashMap uses `equals()`
questions.explanation: Hashtable is an old (legacy) hash-based map, like Vector is a legacy list. Its methods are synchronized, so it is thread-safe but pays a locking cost on every call, which is why HashMap is used in normal code and ConcurrentHashMap when thread safety is needed. Sorted order is TreeMap's feature, and `==` comparison is IdentityHashMap's.

questions.explanation: A TreeSet keeps elements sorted: [10, 23, 50, 80, 90]. `first()` is the smallest (left-most node) and `last()` the largest (right-most node). `headSet(80)` returns the elements strictly less than 80 — the bound is exclusive — so 80 is not included; `[80, 90]` would be `tailSet(80)`.

questions.question: Your application reads configuration like `username=admin` and `password=123` from a file into key-value pairs of Strings. Which specialised map class does the lecture associate with this use case?
questions.explanation: `Properties` is a specialised map (it extends Hashtable) designed for configuration data as String key/value pairs. EnumMap needs enum keys, WeakHashMap is for cache-like entries that can be garbage-collected, and IdentityHashMap compares keys by reference — none of these fit simple config files.

questions.question: `String a = new String("Aditya"); String b = new String("Aditya");` Both are put as keys into a `HashMap` and, separately, into an `IdentityHashMap`. How many entries does each map end up with?
questions.explanation: HashMap is equality-based: `a.equals(b)` is true and their `hashCode()` values match, so the second put replaces the first's value — one entry. IdentityHashMap compares keys with `==`, and `a` and `b` are two distinct objects created with `new`, so it keeps two entries. The reversed option confuses which map uses reference equality.

questions.question: With the TreeSet `[10, 23, 50, 80, 90]`, what does this print?
questions.explanation: `lower(50)` is the greatest element strictly below 50 → 23; `floor(55)` is the greatest element ≤ 55 → 50 (55 itself is not in the set). `higher(90)` needs something strictly above 90, there is none, so it returns null. `ceiling(80)` is the smallest element ≥ 80 → 80 itself, whereas `higher(80)` would give 90.

questions.question: You count tasks per weekday with keys from `enum Day { MON, TUE, WED, ... }`. A reviewer suggests replacing `new HashMap<Day, Integer>()` with `new EnumMap<>(Day.class)`. Which benefit described in the lecture is correct?
options: EnumMap allows a null key for "no day", which HashMap does not
EnumMap is thread-safe, so no synchronization is ever needed
EnumMap sorts entries by the Integer value instead of by key
EnumMap skips hashing (it is array-based on the enum constants), is memory-efficient and iterates in the enum's declaration order
questions.explanation: Because the set of possible keys is fixed, EnumMap can store values in an array indexed by each constant's position — no hashing, compact memory, and iteration order follows the enum (MON, TUE, ...). It does not allow a null key (null values are allowed), the opposite of the first option. It is not synchronized and orders by key, not by value.

questions.question: At startup you load default settings into a `Map<String, String>` that may already contain values the user has customised. Defaults must fill in only missing keys and never overwrite a user's choice. Which call should you use for each default?
questions.explanation: As the lecture's code comment says, `put()` always replaces, while `putIfAbsent()` only inserts when the key is missing and leaves an existing value alone. `replace` does the opposite of what is needed — it only changes keys that already exist. `getOrDefault` just reads a fallback value and never stores anything in the map.

questions.question: For the TreeSet `[10, 23, 50, 80, 90]`, which call returns exactly `[23, 50, 80]`?
questions.explanation: The two-argument `subSet(from, to)` includes `from` but excludes `to`, giving [23, 50]. NavigableSet's overload `subSet(from, fromInclusive, to, toInclusive)` lets you include both ends, giving [23, 50, 80]. `headSet(80)` is everything below 80 ([10, 23, 50]) and `tailSet(23)` is everything from 23 up ([23, 50, 80, 90]).

questions.question: What does this program print? (A TreeMap is used so the printed order is the sorted key order.)
questions.explanation: `putIfAbsent(103, ...)` finds 103 already mapped, changes nothing and returns the existing value "Rohan". `remove(101, "Abhay")` and `replace(102, "Aditya", "Sonu")` only act if the current value matches, and it doesn't (101 is Aditya, 102 is Rohit), so both do nothing. `replace(101, "Sonu")` updates the existing key 101, and `getOrDefault(105, "Unknown")` returns the fallback because 105 is absent.

questions.question: You keep extra metadata for UI objects in a map keyed by those objects. When a UI object is discarded and no longer referenced anywhere else, its entry should disappear automatically instead of keeping the object alive forever. Which map fits, per the lecture?
options: `IdentityHashMap`, because it compares keys by reference
`LinkedHashMap`, because it removes the oldest entry automatically
`EnumMap`, because it is the most memory-efficient map
`WeakHashMap`, because it holds keys through weak references so unused keys can be garbage-collected along with their entries
questions.explanation: A normal map holds strong references to its keys, so the key object can never be collected while it is in the map — a classic memory leak. WeakHashMap holds keys weakly; once nothing else references a key, the garbage collector can reclaim it and the entry vanishes, giving cache-like behaviour. IdentityHashMap only changes how keys are compared, and LinkedHashMap does not evict on its own by default.
